strengths: The paper addresses a very important and challenging problem: exact inversion of diffusion SDEs without the need to store the entire noise realization in memory.

The theoretical framework is elegant, specifically the use of Fisk-Stratonovich integration, exponential integrators, and the Dubins-Schwarz representation theorem to express the stochastic term as a time-changed Brownian bridge (Proposition 4.1).
The application of the coupling-parameter technique from McCallum & Foster (2024) to construct an algebraically reversible SDE solver is well-formulated.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is extremely limited. The paper only contains a single qualitative image interpolation example on a single pair of faces (Figure 1). There are no quantitative metrics (such as reconstruction MSE, PSNR, FID, or computational/memory overhead comparisons).
The paper lacks comparison against relevant baselines, such as the SDE inversion method by Wu & De la Torre (2022) discussed in the related works, or SDEdit.
The proposed method is motivated by applications like image editing and solving continuous adjoint equations for guided generation. However, neither of these applications is implemented or evaluated.

Important hyperparameters, such as the coupling parameter $\zeta$, are not analyzed. It is unclear how different values of $\zeta$ affect the stability, reconstruction error, or visual quality of the samples.

strengths: Novel SDE Inversion Formulation: The paper introduces a novel algebraically reversible solver for diffusion SDEs. Inverting SDEs is notoriously difficult due to the stochastic nature of the path, and this work provides a creative solution.

Solid Theoretical Foundation: The use of the Fisk-Stratonovich integral and the Dubins-Schwarz representation theorem to express the stochastic term as a time-changed Brownian motion is mathematically rigorous and elegant.

Memory Efficiency: By integrating the Brownian interval, the solver avoids the need to store the entire noise realization across all timesteps in memory, which is a major bottleneck in previous SDE inversion methods.
Clear Presentation: The paper is well-written, and the theoretical derivations in the appendix are clear and easy to follow.
weaknesses: Extremely Limited Empirical Evaluation: The experimental section is exceptionally thin, consisting of only a single qualitative figure (Figure 1) showing image interpolation across a few face samples. There are no quantitative metrics (such as MSE/PSNR/SSIM of reconstruction, FID of generated samples, or visual quality metrics).

Lack of Comparative Benchmarks: The paper discusses prior SDE inversion work (e.g., Wu & De la Torre, 2022) in the related works section but does not provide any empirical comparison against it. A quantitative comparison showing the trade-offs in reconstruction accuracy and generation quality is highly necessary.

No Analysis of Computational/Memory Overhead: Although the method claims to not require storing the Wiener process in memory, it introduces augmented states and uses the Brownian interval. The paper lacks runtime and memory benchmarks demonstrating the actual overhead (e.g., step times, peak VRAM) compared to standard solvers.

Idealized Assumptions: The solver construction assumes that the data prediction model is trained to zero loss. In practice, diffusion models always have approximation errors. The paper should evaluate and discuss how robust the proposed reversible solver is to realistic model approximation errors.

Incomplete Paper Length: The main text of the submission is only 4 pages long. The paper leaves out crucial experiments, ablation studies (e.g., sensitivity to the coupling parameter $\zeta$), and analysis that are standard for a full conference paper.

strengths: The paper presents a solid theoretical foundation, successfully combining the Fisk-Stratonovich formulation of diffusion SDEs, the Dubins-Schwarz representation theorem, and exponential integrators to derive an exact solution involving time-changed Brownian motion.
The adaptation of the coupling technique from McCallum & Foster (2024) to SDEs is a neat contribution, resulting in an algebraically reversible scheme that is mathematically elegant.

The integration of Brownian intervals (Kidger et al., 2021) to avoid storing the entire Wiener process in memory is a clever and theoretically sound way to address memory bottleneck challenges in SDE inversion.
weaknesses: The experimental evaluation is extremely minimal, consisting of only a single qualitative image interpolation example in Figure 1. There are no quantitative metrics (such as MSE, PSNR, SSIM, or FID) to evaluate reconstruction accuracy or generation quality.

The main selling point of the proposed method is that it does not require storing the entire realization of the Wiener process in memory. However, the paper lacks any quantitative memory or execution time benchmarks comparing it to noise-storing SDE inversion (e.g., Wu & De la Torre, 2022). This makes it impossible to evaluate the actual practical benefits and computational overhead of using the Brownian interval.

While the introduction and motivation sections highlight key downstream applications such as SDE-based image editing and continuous adjoint-guided generation, none of these applications are empirically tested.

The effect of the coupling parameter $\zeta$ on stability and reconstruction fidelity is not investigated. The stability analysis is left entirely as future work, as acknowledged in the limitations section.
At only 4 pages of main text, the manuscript feels premature and incomplete. It lacks the depth, thorough empirical verification, and rigorous comparisons expected of a full conference paper at ICML.

strengths: Elegant and solid theoretical foundation connecting the literature of neural ODE/SDE reversible solvers (specifically the McCallum-Foster method) with the specialized exponential integrators (Lawson methods) designed for diffusion models.
Unified and highly versatile framework that works for both the probability flow ODE and reverse-time SDE, accommodating both noise-prediction and data-prediction formulations.
Overcomes major limitations of prior diffusion inversion methods (like EDICT, BDIA, and BELM) by providing an arbitrarily high order of convergence and significantly better numerical stability.
Proposes the first exact inversion scheme for diffusion SDEs that does not require storing the entire Brownian motion trajectory in memory, utilizing splittable PRNGs / Brownian intervals.

Extensive and rigorous appendix containing detailed proofs of convergence, derivations, and comprehensive proofs demonstrating how Rex generalizes and subsumes several popular existing solvers (DDIM, DPM-Solver, SEEDS, etc.).

Strong empirical results on image generation (CelebA-HQ) and conditional text-to-image generation (Stable Diffusion v1.5) showcasing excellent generation quality and smooth latent-space interpolation.
weaknesses: Higher computational cost in terms of Number of Function Evaluations (NFEs) due to the reversible coupling mechanism which requires evaluating the neural network multiple times per step, representing a standard trade-off for algebraic reversibility.

The data-prediction formulation can exhibit extreme latent-space instability near $t \to 0$ due to the singularity of the $1/\sigma_t$ terms (as detailed in Appendix J). While the paper addresses this by recommending the noise-prediction formulation or modifying the final steps, a more prominent discussion of this limitation in the main text would benefit practitioners.

The SDE variants of Rex (especially high-order ones using space-time Lévy areas like ShARK) are mathematically complex and require highly specialized SDE libraries, which might limit straightforward out-of-the-box implementation for some users.

strengths: A strong mathematical foundation based on Lawson methods, exponential integrators, and the McCallum-Foster coupling framework.

Provides a unified perspective, showing that the proposed Rex framework subsumes and generalizes several popular diffusion solvers (such as DDIM, DPM-Solver, SEEDS) into their algebraically reversible counterparts.
First framework to achieve exact, memory-efficient inversion for diffusion SDEs without storing the entire Brownian trajectory in memory, utilizing smart PRNG reconstruction methods.

Demonstrates excellent empirical performance, outperforming prior state-of-the-art reversible solvers (like EDICT, BDIA, and BELM) across both unconditional and text-conditioned generation metrics (FID, CLIP, Image Reward).
Extremely thorough appendix containing complete derivations, mathematical proofs, and extensive qualitative results.
weaknesses: The computational cost (number of function evaluations or NFE) of the proposed reversible solvers is not thoroughly discussed in the main text. Reversible schemes typically require extra model evaluations per step, and a clearer discussion of this efficiency trade-off is needed.

The data prediction formulation of the solver exhibits significant instability (as documented in Appendix J and Figure 9, which show failures and overflows in the SDE case). This limitation should be explicitly highlighted in the main text.

While the exact reversibility of SDEs is a key contribution, the paper mostly showcases image interpolation. Demonstrating concrete downstream applications like image editing or localized manipulation would have further strengthened the practical impact of SDE inversion.

strengths: Addresses an important and active research area: exact algebraic inversion of diffusion models for downstream tasks like image editing and interpolation.

Proposes a unified framework (Rex) that handles both the probability flow ODE and the reverse-time SDE using a combination of Lawson exponential integrators and McCallum-Foster style algebraic coupling.
Provides a clever SDE time-change formulation that reduces the reverse-time SDE to an additive-noise SDE, enabling the application of high-order stochastic Runge-Kutta methods like ShARK.
Includes extensive theoretical analysis, including convergence order proofs for both ODE and SDE variants, and a highly detailed appendix detailing connections to existing solvers.
weaknesses: A major discrepancy exists between the presentation focus and practical stability: The main text explicitly focuses on the data prediction parameterization (Page 4). However, Appendix J (Page 56) reveals that this formulation is highly unstable for inversion, exhibiting latent space variances on the order of $10^7$ in the ODE case and complete failure due to overflow in the SDE case (Figure 9). To obtain stable inversions and perform interpolation (Section 5.2), the authors had to switch to the noise prediction parameterization. Sweeping this critical limitation to the appendix while focusing the main text on the unstable variant is a significant presentation and evidential weakness.

The claim of being the first exact SDE inversion method without storing the entire Brownian path is somewhat overstated in terms of novelty, as the path reconstruction relies entirely on existing frameworks such as Virtual Brownian Trees (Li et al., 2020) and Brownian Intervals (Kidger et al., 2021).

In terms of unconditional image generation (Table 1), Rex does not demonstrate a clear or consistent advantage over existing reversible baselines. For instance, O-BELM achieves better FID scores at 10 and 20 steps compared to both Rex (RK4) and Rex (Euler-Maruyama).

The paper lacks a comprehensive discussion of the computational cost and Number of Function Evaluations (NFE) trade-offs. Since reversible solvers require auxiliary states and additional evaluations, an explicit comparison of NFE vs. performance against both standard and reversible baselines is necessary.
